details: RBMK reactor fleet history: total RBMK-1000 units constructed: 17; RBMK-1500 (larger version; Ignalina Lithuania): 2; total: 19 RBMK reactors built; first RBMK-1000: Leningrad NPP Unit 1 (1973); design origin: Dollezhal (NIKIET) + Alexandrov (Kurchatov Institute) + Minenergo (Ministry of Energy); RBMK advantages that drove Soviet adoption: (1) Can be refueled while at power (on-line refueling vs PWR shutdown for refueling); (2) Uses natural uranium or slightly enriched (initial: 2.0%) → no large enrichment capacity required; (3) Modular construction (no large pressure vessel forging needed; Soviet industry limitation); (4) Simple design: channels + graphite + boiling water; (5) Large unit size (1000 MWe, then 1500 MWe); RBMK disadvantages (partially known pre-1986): positive void coefficient; no containment; large complex graphite moderator; graphite fire risk; poor emergency response design

details: Leningrad NPP history: first RBMK-1000 → first commercial nuclear power in USSR; Unit 1: first power 1973; commercial operation 1974; 1975 accident (classified): during startup test; partial fuel channel failure; power excursion; no public disclosure; classified; NOT shared with other RBMK plants; later identified as: first indication of void coefficient + graphite tip dynamics = same conditions as Chernobyl 1986; Unit 2-4: 1975-1981; RBMK-1000 standard design; 44 years operation; accumulated 800+ TWh electricity; post-Chernobyl modifications: all applied by 1987-1990 (SCRAM 12s; ORM 15 minimum formalized; graphite absorber tip replaced; enrichment increased 2.0→2.8%); decommissioning: Leningrad replacement units: VVER-1200 (Gen III+; passive safety; double containment): Unit 5 online 2017; Unit 6 online 2020; all 4 RBMK units cold shutdown 2018-2020; site: dual RBMK (decommissioning) + VVER (operating) = unique transition
